Residual correlations between the series of a fitted model

Source: R/residual_cor.R
residual_cor.Rd

Posterior correlations, covariances and optional partial correlations between the series' latent trends. Residual here means the co-variation of the trends left once the covariate effects are accounted for. residuals.mvgam() returns the observation residuals. Three kinds of trend estimate these correlations:

  • A factor trend (n_lv on the trend constructor). Each draw gives the series covariance Z Omega Z', with Z the loadings and Omega the covariance of the latent states. mvn() and mvt() add each series' residual variance to the diagonal: Psi^2, or Psi^2 * nu / (nu - 2) under mvt().

  • A trend with correlated innovations: RW(), AR(), CAR() or ZMVN() with cor = TRUE, or VAR().

  • A hierarchical trend (gr on the trend constructor).

Usage

residual_cor(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mvgam'
residual_cor(
  object,
  covariance = c("stationary", "innovation"),
  by_group = FALSE,
  partial = FALSE,
  summary = TRUE,
  robust = FALSE,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975),
  ndraws = NULL,
  draw_ids = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A fitted mvgam object.

...

Unused. Anything passed here is refused.

covariance

Which covariance to summarise. "stationary" (the default) gives the covariance of the latent states over the whole series. "innovation" gives the covariance of one time step's innovations. The two coincide for a trend whose states keep no memory between times.

by_group

Logical, for a hierarchical trend. FALSE (the default) returns the population correlation of the innovations, tcrossprod(L_Omega_global), under either covariance. TRUE also returns each group's correlation, alpha * tcrossprod(L_global) + (1 - alpha) * tcrossprod(L_dev[g]).

partial

Logical. TRUE also computes partial correlations, P_ij = -inv(R)_ij / sqrt(inv(R)_ii * inv(R)_jj). A partial correlation measures the association of two series once every other series is held fixed. The result stores them in the fields whose names start with prec. A factor fit with fewer factors than series has a singular covariance of rank n_lv and is refused. shared_variation() reports the variation its series share. The residual variances of mvn() and mvt() make their covariance full rank.

summary

Logical. TRUE (the default) summarises each entry: the point estimate, spread, credible interval and posterior sign probabilities. FALSE returns the arrays of draws.

robust

Logical. If FALSE (the default), uses mean and standard deviation for summaries. If TRUE, uses median and median absolute deviation (MAD).

probs

Two probabilities for the lower and upper bounds of the credible interval. Default c(0.025, 0.975), a 95% interval.

ndraws

Positive integer specifying number of posterior draws to use. NULL (default) uses all available draws.

draw_ids

Optional integer vector selecting a subset of posterior draw indices to use. NULL (default) uses all draws (subject to ndraws).

Value

An mvgam_residcor object. Under by_group = TRUE on a hierarchical trend, an mvgam_residcor_list of them: the population matrix as "_global" and one per group. plot.mvgam_residcor_list() draws them as faceted heatmaps.

Details

A correlated-innovation trend gives each draw the covariance diag(sigma) L_Omega L_Omega' diag(sigma). A VAR() trend takes the leading block of Omega_trend, the stationary covariance the Stan model derives from Phi_trend, Sigma_trend and, under ma = TRUE, Theta_trend.

The stationary covariance describes the states over the whole series. An AR(cor = TRUE) trend reports the stationary covariance of its states, including any moving-average term. With one lag it is Sigma[a, b] / (1 - ar_a * ar_b). A CAR() trend holds it at every time of an irregular grid. A draw whose autoregression is explosive has no stationary covariance and keeps its innovation covariance. A warning gives the count once per session. ZMVN() keeps no memory between times and RW() has no stationary distribution. Both report their innovation covariance. A hierarchical AR() converts each group's scales to stationary scales in the same way, before its global and group correlations are mixed.

Under covariance = "innovation" a VAR() fit reports the contemporaneous shocks. Its transition matrix spreads each shock across series at every step. The two correlations can differ substantially.

Intervals and spreads of correlations are computed on the Fisher-z scale, atanh(r), then back-transformed. The intervals stay inside (-1, 1). The reported matrix summarises each entry separately. It need not be positive semi-definite, most visibly when a few factors drive many series. A computation that factorises the matrix, such as chol(), takes summary = FALSE, whose per-draw matrices are valid correlation matrices. prob_positive and prob_negative are posterior sign probabilities. prob_nonzero is the larger of the two. sig_cor keeps the correlations whose prob_nonzero exceeds prob_threshold, fixed at 0.95. Its other entries are zero.

jsdgam() fits the same factor model. Its species covariance follows the factor rule above.

References

Hui, F. K. C. (2016). boral - Bayesian Ordination and Regression Analysis of Multivariate Abundance Data in R. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 7(6), 744-750. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.12514

See also

plot.mvgam_residcor() draws the matrix as a heatmap. summary.mvgam_residcor() lists the pairs. ordinate() draws the loadings as a biplot. The example of trend_constructors takes the correlations of a CAR(cor = TRUE) trend. The joint species distribution article interprets species correlations from a factor model.

Other latent dynamics: active_factors(), compare_loadings(), fevd.mvgam(), irf.mvgam(), ordinate(), posterior_transition_matrix(), shared_variation(), stability.mvgam()

Examples

# \dontrun{
# Detections of 6 species whose occupancy shares two latent factors
simdat <- sim_closure_unit_data(family = occ(), n_species = 6L,
                                n_sites = 80L, n_visits = 4L,
                                n_lv = 2L, seed = 1L)
mod <- jsdgam(formula = bf(y ~ series * env, p ~ series + tod_c),
              factor_formula = ~ -1,
              data = simdat$data_train, family = occ(),
              n_lv = 2L, chains = 2, silent = 2)
#> Warning: 1051 of 2000 (53.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
#> Warning: 1 of 2000 (0.0%) transitions hit the maximum treedepth limit of 10.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.

# Species correlations after the fixed effects
rc <- residual_cor(mod)
round(rc$cor, 2)
#>      sp_1  sp_2  sp_3 sp_4  sp_5  sp_6
#> sp_1 1.00  0.27  0.33 0.65  0.42  0.65
#> sp_2 0.27  1.00  0.85 0.62 -0.74 -0.21
#> sp_3 0.33  0.85  1.00 0.82 -0.53 -0.07
#> sp_4 0.65  0.62  0.82 1.00  0.06  0.35
#> sp_5 0.42 -0.74 -0.53 0.06  1.00  0.77
#> sp_6 0.65 -0.21 -0.07 0.35  0.77  1.00
plot(rc)


# Next: summary(rc) lists the pairs by posterior sign probability
# }
